issues.legal_issue: A crude shed or hut let for non-residential use falls within the statutory meaning of a building.
material_facts: The lease included a structure measuring about 600 square feet together with the land and a well.
The lessor-owned structure was to be retained and returned to the lessor, and the lessee used it in connection with the petrol business.
The structure was capable of use for residential or non-residential purposes.
issues.conclusion: The kaichalai was a building within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(2) includes a building or hut let for residential or non-residential purposes. Because the Act applies to both kinds of use, “hut” is not limited to a dwelling; it includes a crude shed or similar construction usable for any purpose.

predicates.rent_control_building_classification_cas: The proceeding required classification of a structure under a regime regulating the letting of buildings.
predicates.structure_is_shed_or_hut: The property included a shed, hut, or similarly crude construction.
predicates.structure_is_let: The lessor included the structure in the property let to the lessee.

issues.definition: When a proceeding requires classification of a let structure under a building-rental regime, a shed or hut included in the letting qualifies as a building.

issues.legal_issue: A composite letting of land and a building is governed as a letting of a building when the parties intended the land and building to go together, and the lease cannot be divided without a clear contrary intention.
material_facts: The original lease included vacant land, a well, and the lessor-owned structure as one letting.
The lease required the lessee to remove the structures he had put up but to return the lessor-owned structure without damage.
The structure was of substantial size, was used in connection with the lessee’s business, and was treated in the lease documents as a material part of the property.
The surrounding circumstances supported the inference that the lessor intended to let the land and structure together; the lease did not clearly express an intention to separate them.
issues.conclusion: The letting was a composite lease of land and building within the scope of the Rent Control Act, and it could not be dissected into separate land and building leases in the absence of a clear contrary intention.
issues.legal_principle: In a composite lease, the court should consider whether the parties intended the land and building to go together and whether the lessor could have intended to let the land without the building; the dominant-purpose test is not invariably helpful. Section 2(2) includes land let along with a building, and a joint letting should not be split in the absence of a clear intention in the deed. The Court drew assistance from Sultan Bros. P. Ltd. v. C.I.T. on inseparable letting, considered Larsen & Toubro and the other composite-leasing authorities, and distinguished the extreme proposition that any building on leased land automatically brings the whole lease within rent control, as well as the reliance placed on Irani v. Chidambaram Chettiar and Salay Mohd. Sait v. J.M.S. Charity.

rule.if: composite_lease_classification_case and land_and_building_leased_together and parties_intended_joint_enjoyment and not clear_intention_to_separate

predicates.composite_lease_classification_case: The proceeding required classification of a letting that included both land and a building.
predicates.land_and_building_leased_together: The lessor included both land and a building in the same letting.
predicates.parties_intended_joint_enjoyment: The lease terms and surrounding circumstances showed that the parties intended the land and building to go together.
predicates.clear_intention_to_separate: The lease clearly expressed an intention to separate the building letting from the land letting.

issues.definition: When a classification proceeding concerns land and a building leased together, the parties intended joint enjoyment, and no clear intention to separate them appears, the composite letting is treated as a building letting.
